title.en: T'ang Asks Hsia Ko Whether Things Existed in the Beginning (Liezi)
title.zh: 殷湯問於夏革：古初有物乎？（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The court of T'ang of Yin (Anyang, Henan, China)

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist? asks T'ang of Yin. If things did not exist then, how could they be in existence now? replies Hsia Ko — to the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit; beginning may be end, and end may be beginning; but when it comes to something outside matter in space or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us.
summary.zh: 殷湯問於夏革曰：古初有物乎？夏革曰：古初無物，今惡得物——物之始終，初無極已；始或為終，終或為始。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; a priority Creation & Cosmology dialogue. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: T'ANG of Yin questioned Hsia Ko, saying: "In the beginnings of antiquity, did individual things exist?" "If things did not exist then," replied Hsia Ko, "how could they be in existence now? Or will the men of future ages be right in denying the existence of things at the present time?" "Things in that case," pursued T'ang, "have no before nor after?" Hsia Ko replied: "To the beginning and end of things there is no precise limit. Beginning may be end, and end may be beginning. How can we conceive of any fixed period to either?

But when it comes to something outside matter in space, or anterior to events in time, our knowledge fails us." "Then, upwards and downwards and in every direction space is a finite quantity?" Ko replied: "I do not know." T'ang asked the question again with more insistence, and Ko said: "It may be that space is infinite, or it may be that it is limited. How can I tell? But beyond infinity there must again exist non-infinity, and within the unlimited again that which is not unlimited.

title.en: The Outer Shell That Encloses Heaven and Earth (Liezi)
title.zh: 四海之外，六合之外（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The lands beyond the Four Seas (symbolic pin: Yantai, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 四海之外（象徵定位：山東煙臺）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: What is there beyond the Four Seas? Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i — Hsia Ko travelled east to Ying and west to Pin and found the inhabitants nowise different. The lesser is always enclosed by a greater without ever reaching an end: heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell that is infinite and immeasurable.
summary.zh: 四海之外奚若？曰：猶齊州也——大猶含小，終無窮已；天地含物之體，亦自含於太虛。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: T'ang continued his inquiries, saying: "What is there beyond the Four Seas?" Ko replied: "Just what there is here in the province of Ch'i." "How can you prove that?" asked T'ang. "When travelling eastwards," said Ko, "I came to the land of Ying, where the inhabitants were nowise different from those in this part of the country. I inquired about the countries east of Ying, and found that they, too, were similar to their neighbour. Travelling westwards, I came to Pin, where the inhabitants were similar to our own countrymen. ... That is how I know that the regions within the Four Seas, the Four Wildernesses and the Four Uttermost Ends of the Earth are nowise different from the country we ourselves inhabit.

Thus, the lesser is always enclosed by a greater, without ever reaching an end. Heaven and earth, which enclose the myriad objects of creation, are themselves enclosed in some outer shell. Enclosing heaven and earth and the myriad objects within them, this outer shell is infinite and immeasurable. How do we know but that there is some mightier universe in existence outside our own? That is a question to which we can give no answer.

title.en: Nü Kua's Five-Coloured Stones and Kung Kung's Snapped Pillar (Liezi)
title.zh: 女媧鍊五色石補天，共工觸不周山（列子湯問篇）

region.en: Mount Pu-chou and the leaning heavens (mythic NW; symbolic pin: Jiayuguan, Gansu, China)
region.zh: 不周山（神話西北；象徵定位：甘肅嘉峪關）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Heaven and earth are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect: Nü Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts, and cut off the legs of the Ao to support the four corners of the heavens. Later, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsü for the throne and blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth — that is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, and why all rivers roll to the south-east.
summary.zh: 天地亦物也——女媧氏鍊五色石以補其闕，斷鼇足以立四極；共工氏與顓頊爭為帝，怒而觸不周之山，折天柱，絕地維。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the Nü Kua repair-myth cross-linked to the chinese tradition's Huainanzi record of the same story. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Heaven and earth, then, are themselves only material objects, and therefore imperfect. Hence it is that Nii Kua of old fashioned many-coloured blocks of stone to repair the defective parts. He cut off the legs of the Ao and used them to support the four corners of the heavens.

Later on, Kung Kung fought with Chuan Hsu for the throne, and, blundering in his rage against Mount Pu-chou, he snapped the pillar which connects Heaven and earth. That is why Heaven dips downwards to the north-west, so that sun, moon and stars travel towards that quarter. The earth, on the other hand, is now not large enough to fill up the south-east, so that all rivers and streams roll in that direction.

title.en: The Exchange of Hearts Performed by Pien-ch'iao (Liezi)

region.en: The clinic of the great physician (symbolic pin: Zhengzhou, Henan, China)
region.zh: 扁鵲之診（象徵定位：河南鄭州）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Kung-hu of Lu and Ch'i-ying of Chao both fall ill and are cured by Pien-ch'iao — who then offers to grapple with each man's congenital disease: your mental powers are strong but your character is weak, says he to Kung-hu; his are weak while his character is strong. A potion of medicated wine throws them into a three-day death-like trance, and each man's heart is placed in the other's body — leading to a lawsuit between the two families.
summary.zh: 魯公扈趙齊嬰俱疾，扁鵲遂飲二人毒酒，迷死三日；剖胸探心，易而置之——辭而歸，則公扈反齊嬰之室。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the heart-exchange tale is a landmark of Chinese medical myth. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Pien-ch'iao turned to Kung-hu. "Your mental powers," he said, "are strong, but your character is weak. Hence, though fruitful in plans, you are lacking in decision. Ch'i-ying's mental powers, on the other hand, are weak, while his character is strong. Hence there is want of forethought, and he is placed at a disadvantage by the narrowness of his aim. Now, if I can effect an exchange of hearts between you, the good will be equally balanced in both."

So saying, Pien-ch'iao administered to each of them a potion of medicated wine, which threw them into a death-like trance lasting three days. Then, making an incision in their breasts, he took out each man's heart and placed it in the other's body, poulticing the wounds with herbs of marvellous efficacy. When the two men regained consciousness, they looked exactly the same as before; and, taking their leave, they returned home. Only it was Kung-hu who went to Ch'i-ying's house, where Ch'i-ying's wife and children naturally did not recognise him, while Ch'i-ying went to Kung-hu's house and was not recognised either. This led to a lawsuit between the two families, and Pien-ch'iao was called in as arbitrator. On his explaining how the matter stood, peace was once more restored.

title.en: The Three Magic Swords and the Blood-Feud That Could Not Kill (Liezi)
title.zh: 孔周三劍：含光、承影、宵練（列子湯問篇）

region.en: The house of K'ung Chou of Wei (Anyang region, Henan, China)
region.zh: 衛孔周之家（象徵定位：河南安陽一帶）

texts.period: Liezi, compiled 4th c. BCE-4th c. CE (trans. Lionel Giles, 1912)

source.work: Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzŭ, trans. Lionel Giles, Book V (The Questions of T'ang)

summary.en: Lai Tan, whose body is slight but whose spirit is fierce, seeks the blood of Hei Luan and borrows one of K'ung Chou's three Yin-Emperor swords — Light-absorber, Shadow-container, Night-tempered. He cuts clean through Hei Luan's body in three places, but the victim is quite unconscious of it; the son laughs that he is merely motioning in a silly way with his hand — the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.
summary.zh: 來丹請於衛孔周，得宵練之劍；三斬黑卵之頸——黑卵不覺；其子曰：汝以指揮吾手何也？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon; the sword allegory satirises the vendetta. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: This Hei Luan was the most ferocious character of his day, and in brute strength he was a match for a hundred men. His bones and sinews, skin and flesh were cast in superhuman mould. He would stretch out his neck to the blade or bare his breast to the arrow, but the sharp steel would bend or break, and his body show no scar from the impact.

"I have three swords," replied K'ung Chou, "but with none of them can you kill a man. You may choose which you like. First, however, let me describe their qualities. The first sword is called 'Light-absorber.' It is invisible to the eye, and when you swing it you cannot tell that there is anything there. Things struck by it retain an unbroken surface, and it will pass through a man's body without his knowing it. The second is called 'Shadow-container.' ... The third is called 'Night-tempered,' because in broad daylight you only see its shadow and not the brightness of its blade, while at night you see not the sword itself but the dazzling light which it emits.

Grasping his new weapon, Lai Tan now sought out his enemy, and found him lying in a drunken stupor at his window. He cut clean through his body in three places between the neck and the navel, but Hei Luan was quite unconscious of it. ... And happening to meet Hei Luan's son at the door, he struck at him three times with his sword. But it was like hitting the empty air. Hei Luan's son laughed and said: "Why are you motioning to me in that silly way with your hand?" Thus, the improper use of divine weapons only leads to discomfiture.
